newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soy imports to dwarf current sales to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Brazil soy imports to dwarf current sales to U.S..

text.p: Soybean prices tumbled this week after Cargill Inc said it was importing Brazilian beans to process in the U.S., but Brazil will more than compensate with larger-than-usual U.S. soybean imports this year, analysts said.
The Cargill shipment totaled an estimated 7.2 million bushels, or around four cargoes, according to traders here.
This figure dwindles in comparison with the 700,000 to one million tonnes of soybean which crushers expect Brazil to start importing once the U.S. harvest comes on stream.

"There's talk that Cargill has already bought beans to import later in the year," said Tarcisio Minetto, economist at the Rio Grande do Sul cooperative federation Fecotrigo. "There will be a shortage for crushing."
In addition to crushers and processors buying beans, end-users may also import soymeal and soyoil, according to Carlos Cogo, economist at Agromercados.

"Nowadays crushing margins within Brazil are not viable," he said. "It could be more profitable for the end-user to import soymeal or soyoil directly rather than bringing in the beans and then having to crush them over here."
Although importing soybeans is no novelty for Brazil, one of the world's largest producers, it usually buys practically all the product from Mercosur partners Paraguay and Argentina.
But with a lower-than-expected crop in Argentina this year, Brazil could import in excess of one million tonnes from the U.S. in 1997/98, Cogo estimated.

"At the moment Brazil's purchases are concentrated within the Mercosur. But this year, with estimated imports of 1.8 to 2.0 million tonnes and exports of 8.5 million tonnes, all these import scenarios have to be re-evaluated," he said.
Meanwhile, with prices receding both on the Chicago commodities exchange and domestically, Brazilian farmers are torn between two options.

Either they sell as much of the current crop as possible, taking advantage of any peaks in prices, or they hold on to the product until the second semester when domestic supply is tight and prices traditionally improve.

"They're tearing their hair out," said Minetto. "That is the preoccupation now, because growers are always living with the expectation of earning more. Very few of them enter into fixed price contracts, it's not the culture here."

Farmers had sold 57 percent of their expected total crop in Rio Grande do Sul by the week ending May 29, compared with a national level of 76 percent, according to independent consultants Safras e Mercado.
"This is a good level -- there has never been more than 70 percent sold by this time of the year," said Minetto.
Producers in the southern state were receiving 15.90 to 16.00 reais per 60-kg bag, compared to 16.50 reais a week ago.
